In 1825 King Charles X of France demanded that Haiti pay 150 million francs to compensate French slave owners, in return for recognising its independence. French warships waited off Port-au-Prince as President Jean-Pierre Boyer agreed.

The sum was later cut to 90 million, but Haiti had to borrow from French banks to pay it, adding interest. Paying off the indemnity and the loans taken to cover it took until 1947, and they swallowed a large part of state revenue for generations.

Historians and economists see the debt as a lasting drag on Haiti's growth. In 2003 President Aristide demanded restitution from France, which refused. The debt still shapes how Haitians see the independence they won.
